question: How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?

task_plan.description: Explain the role of tracing, evaluations, and Signals and how they relate to and fit together with each other.
task_plan.request_quote: How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?

answer:
Tracing records what your application or agent does, evaluations measure it against curated test cases, and Signals score the recorded agent activity in production. The docs I read don't state this three-way relationship in one place, so the linking below is my synthesis of their separate descriptions.

- **Tracing (the data layer).** Weave has two tracing paths. Agent integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls and tool calls, and show them in the Agents view. LLM-application integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Calls in the Traces view [S3].
- **Evaluations (pre-release measurement).** An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions. You run it against a `Model` or a custom function, and each `.evaluate()` call is an evaluation run. The goal is to measure behavior on repeatable examples, compare changes over time, and spot regressions [S2].
- **Signals (production monitoring of agents).** In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for agent conversations. Signals score agent turns and surface quality and safety issues, such as a frustrated user or NSFW content, so you can find the traces that need attention [S1].

**How they fit together**
1. Tracing comes first. Agent signals work on the agent trace data that tracing captures. The Agent Lens note says it uses the same trace data as Weave, so traces you already send appear there [S1].
2. Evaluations and Signals are both forms of scoring. Evaluations score a fixed, curated dataset, which suits testing before release. Signals score real agent turns, which suits production [S1][S2].
3. A typical loop would be: trace your agent, use evaluations to test changes, and use Signals to find problems in live traffic. This loop is my interpretation, not a documented procedure.

**Caveat:** An older "Monitors" page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. It says new implementations should use Signals under Weave for Agents [S4]. I haven't mixed the two workflows here.

I didn't read the setup pages for Signals or the agent tracing pages. Ask if you want those steps.

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). * **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

Tracing records what your application or agent does, evaluations measure it against curated test cases, and Signals score the recorded agent activity in production. The docs I read don't state this three-way relationship in one place, so the linking below is my synthesis of their separate descriptions.

- **Evaluations (pre-release measurement).** An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions. You run it against a `Model` or a custom function, and each `.evaluate()` call is an evaluation run. The goal is to measure behavior on repeatable examples, compare changes over time, and spot regressions [S2].
- **Signals (production monitoring of agents).** In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for agent conversations. Signals score agent turns and surface quality and safety issues, such as a frustrated user or NSFW content, so you can find the traces that need attention [S1].

**How they fit together**
1. Tracing comes first. Agent signals work on the agent trace data that tracing captures. The Agent Lens note says it uses the same trace data as Weave, so traces you already send appear there [S1].

3. A typical loop would be: trace your agent, use evaluations to test changes, and use Signals to find problems in live traffic. This loop is my interpretation, not a documented procedure.

**Caveat:** An older "Monitors" page describes a previous approach to production monitoring. It says new implementations should use Signals under Weave for Agents. I haven't mixed the two workflows here.

# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.
